ch25.anchor: took a name from the sound of that number
ch25.note: The Awakening Society (Juewu She), founded at Nankai in September 1919, drew lots to give each member a number and formed a pen name from a near-homophone of it. Deng Yingchao drew number one and took “Yihao”; Zhou Enlai drew number five (wu) and took “Wu Hao,” writing the numeral five, 五, with its homophone 伍. The whole forgery in this chapter turns on this pen name, which Zhou used his life long. Corroborated by published accounts of the society.

ch25.anchor: Zhang Chong, chief secretary of the intelligence subsection of the Investigation Section
ch25.note: Zhang Chong (1904–1941) ran intelligence in the Investigation Section of the Kuomintang Central Party Headquarters, the body that grew into the Zhongtong, and organized the forged notice. In a turn of history he became, from 1937, the Kuomintang’s chief liaison to the Chinese Communist Party and to Zhou Enlai during the second united front; when he died in 1941 Zhou helped mourn him. Corroborated.

ch25.anchor: proved powerfully, that Comrade Zhou Enlai was innocent.
ch25.note: Author’s note. Qin Jie, “A Few Things about Comrade Chen Yangshan in Nanjing,” in In Memory of Chen Yangshan, p. 53.

ch25.anchor: is entitled to make a statement.
ch25.note: Author’s note. “My Career as a Secret Agent and What I Saw and Heard,” in Secret Records of Zhongtong Agents, p. 14.

ch25.anchor: the Lin Biao and Jiang Qing counter-revolutionary cliques, who saw Zhou Enlai
ch25.note: The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) was the mass upheaval Mao Zedong launched; see the earlier notes. Lin Biao was Mao’s designated successor until his death fleeing China in 1971; Jiang Qing, Mao’s wife, led the radical faction later condemned as the “Gang of Four” (Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen). They revived the 1932 forgery to attack Zhou Enlai, and in Mao’s own hands it became, as scholars have put it, a sword hanging over Zhou’s head.

ch25.anchor: was Kang Sheng's alias at the time
ch25.note: Kang Sheng (1898–1975), later head of Party security and a power in the Cultural Revolution, had himself been named in the Kuomintang’s 1931 bounty notice alongside Zhou Enlai, under this very alias, Zhao Rong, and had helped rebut the forgery in 1932. He thus knew first-hand that it was fake, yet kept silent while it was turned against Zhou during the Cultural Revolution; that silence is the author’s point in quoting his earlier written testimony here.

ch25.anchor: Nor did anyone ever mention the matter to him afterward.
ch25.note: Author’s note. The Blurred Screen (Menghu de yingping), pp. 127–128. The author introduces this passage as Li Yimang’s recollection, but the cited title is the memoir of Huang Mulan (Huang Dinghui), the very woman who, as the text relates, engaged the barrister; the attribution in the source is inconsistent.

ch25.anchor: the Tiananmen Incident that would bury the
ch25.note: The Tiananmen Incident of April 5, 1976: during the Qingming festival huge crowds gathered in Tiananmen Square to mourn Zhou Enlai, who had died that January, and in wreaths and poems to denounce the Gang of Four. The authorities suppressed it and branded it “counter-revolutionary”; the verdict was reversed in 1978. The Gang of Four fell in October 1976, a month after Mao’s death.

ch26.anchor: a surprise attack on the Soviet Union around June 20, 1941
ch26.note: Yan Baohang (1895–1968), a Christian activist turned secret Communist working inside Nationalist circles, is said to have learned of the coming German invasion at a Chongqing banquet in June 1941 and passed word to Zhou Enlai, who relayed it to Moscow through the Comintern. The warning is attested in Chinese accounts and the date given is strikingly accurate; the further claim that it let the Red Army stand to twenty-four hours early and drew Stalin’s personal thanks is the Chinese record’s own, and is not confirmed by Western scholarship, which notes that Stalin disregarded many such warnings, Richard Sorge’s among them. Take the contribution as corroborated, its decisive effect as uncorroborated.

ch26.anchor: and even named the date, June 21, 1941.
ch26.note: Author’s note. Hua Pu, comp. and trans., “An Account of Major Events in the Chinese Revolution in The Dimitrov Diary,” Studies in CCP History (Zhonggong Dangshi Yanjiu), 2001, no. 5.

ch26.anchor: may be called the 'Three Later Heroes,'
ch26.note: The “Three Heroes of Longtan” (see the earlier note), Qian Zhuangfei, Li Kenong, and Hu Di, who penetrated the Kuomintang’s secret service around 1930, were Zhou Enlai’s “Three Earlier Heroes.” Xiong Xianghui, Chen Zhongjing, and Shen Jian, who from the late 1930s worked inside Hu Zongnan’s headquarters, were the “Three Later Heroes.”

ch26.anchor: if medals were given, they should be given to you too.
ch26.note: Author’s note. Xiong Xianghui, My Career in Intelligence and Diplomacy, CCP History Press, 1999, p. 99.

ch26.anchor: vanishing in a moment into the oppressive night of old China.
ch26.note: Author’s note. Zhang Kexia, “The Secret Post,” in Materials on Revolutionary History, no. 3, Literary and Historical Materials Press, 1981.

ch26.anchor: led more than 23,000 men in revolt in the Tai'erzhuang and Zaozhuang area.
ch26.note: Zhang Kexia (1900–1984) and He Jifeng, both secret Communists inside the Nationalist forces, brought their troops over on the eve of the Huaihai Campaign in November 1948; the defection opened a gap in the Nationalist line and is counted a significant factor in that decisive battle. Corroborated.

ch26.note: Author’s note. Lin Cong, “A Brief Life of Li Kenong,” CCP History Materials, no. 57.

ch27.anchor: as Comrade Chen Geng in Shanghai
ch27.note: Comrade Chen Geng in Shanghai (1980) was the author’s earlier study, written as part of the multi-volume biography General Chen Geng; the present book grew out of it. Chen Geng, a founding officer of the Central Special Section, is a central figure of the earlier chapters.
